
Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

### DnsCaaRecord <a name="DnsCaaRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsCaaRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS CAA Record implementation.

CAA records specify which Certificate Authorities are authorized to issue
certificates for a domain. This record type is only available in Public DNS Zones.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create a CAA record to authorize Let's Encrypt:
const caaRecord = new DnsCaaRecord(this, "caa-record", {
  name: "@",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { flags: 0, tag: "issue", value: "letsencrypt.org" },
    { flags: 0, tag: "issuewild", value: ";" }, // Disallow wildcard certs
    { flags: 0, tag: "iodef", value: "mailto:security@example.com" },
  ],
});
```

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsCaaRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnszone } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnszone.DnsCaaRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsCaaRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsCnameRecord <a name="DnsCnameRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsCnameRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS CNAME Record implementation.

CNAME records create an alias from one hostname to another.
Supports alias records via targetResourceId for pointing to Azure resources.
Note: CNAME records cannot coexist with other record types at the same name.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create a CNAME record:
const cnameRecord = new DnsCnameRecord(this, "alias-record", {
  name: "app",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsCnameRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsCnameRecord } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsCnameRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsCnameRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsCnameRecord <a name="DnsCnameRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsCnameRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS CNAME Record implementation.

CNAME records create an alias from one hostname to another.
Supports alias records via targetResourceId for pointing to Azure resources.
Note: CNAME records cannot coexist with other record types at the same name.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create a CNAME record:
const cnameRecord = new DnsCnameRecord(this, "alias-record", {
  name: "app",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  cname: "www.example.com",
});
```

### DnsForwardingRuleset <a name="DnsForwardingRuleset" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsForwardingRuleset"></a>

Unified Azure DNS Forwarding Ruleset implementation.

This class provides a unified implementation for creating DNS Forwarding Rulesets
that enable conditional forwarding of DNS queries. Rulesets work with DNS Resolver
Outbound Endpoints to route queries to specific target DNS servers based on domain names.

Key Requirements:
- Requires at least one DNS Resolver Outbound Endpoint
- Each ruleset can contain up to 1000 forwarding rules
- Regional resource (must match outbound endpoint location)
- Can be linked to multiple virtual networks

*Example*

```typescript
// DNS forwarding ruleset with explicit version pinning:
const ruleset = new DnsForwardingRuleset(this, "ruleset", {
  name: "my-ruleset",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  dnsResolverOutboundEndpointIds: [outboundEndpoint.id],
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01",
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsForwardingRuleset.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsForwardingRuleset } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsForwardingRuleset.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsForwardingRuleset.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsForwardingRuleset <a name="DnsForwardingRuleset" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsforwardingruleset.DnsForwardingRuleset"></a>

Unified Azure DNS Forwarding Ruleset implementation.

This class provides a unified implementation for creating DNS Forwarding Rulesets
that enable conditional forwarding of DNS queries. Rulesets work with DNS Resolver
Outbound Endpoints to route queries to specific target DNS servers based on domain names.

Key Requirements:
- Requires at least one DNS Resolver Outbound Endpoint
- Each ruleset can contain up to 1000 forwarding rules
- Regional resource (must match outbound endpoint location)
- Can be linked to multiple virtual networks

*Example*

```typescript
// DNS forwarding ruleset with explicit version pinning:
const ruleset = new DnsForwardingRuleset(this, "ruleset", {
  name: "my-ruleset",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  dnsResolverOutboundEndpointIds: [outboundEndpoint.id],
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01",
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsforwardingruleset.DnsForwardingRuleset.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnsforwardingruleset } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnsforwardingruleset.DnsForwardingRuleset.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsforwardingruleset.DnsForwardingRuleset.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink <a name="DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink"></a>

Azure DNS Forwarding Ruleset Virtual Network Link implementation.

Virtual Network Links connect DNS Forwarding Rulesets to virtual networks,
enabling those VNets to use the conditional forwarding rules defined in the ruleset.
This allows VMs and other resources in the linked VNets to resolve domains according
to the forwarding rules.

*Example*

```typescript
// Virtual network link with explicit version:
const link = new DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink(this, "vnet-link", {
  name: "my-vnet-link",
  dnsForwardingRulesetId: ruleset.id,
  virtualNetworkId: vnet.id,
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01"
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsforwardingruleset.DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnsforwardingruleset } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnsforwardingruleset.DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsforwardingruleset.DnsForwardingRulesetVirtualNetworkLink.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsMxRecord <a name="DnsMxRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsMxRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS MX Record implementation.

MX records specify mail exchange servers for a domain.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create an MX record:
const mxRecord = new DnsMxRecord(this, "mail-record", {
  name: "@",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { preference: 10, exchange: "mail1.example.com" },
    { preference: 20, exchange: "mail2.example.com" },
  ],
});
```

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

Any object.

### DnsMxRecord <a name="DnsMxRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsMxRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS MX Record implementation.

MX records specify mail exchange servers for a domain.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create an MX record:
const mxRecord = new DnsMxRecord(this, "mail-record", {
  name: "@",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { preference: 10, exchange: "mail1.example.com" },
    { preference: 20, exchange: "mail2.example.com" },
  ],
});
```


Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

### DnsNsRecord <a name="DnsNsRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsNsRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS NS Record implementation.

NS records specify the authoritative name servers for a domain or subdomain.
This record type is only available in Public DNS Zones.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create an NS record for a subdomain delegation:
const nsRecord = new DnsNsRecord(this, "ns-record", {
  name: "subdomain",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { nsdname: "ns1.subdomain.example.com" },
    { nsdname: "ns2.subdomain.example.com" },
  ],
});
```

Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsNsRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsNsRecord } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsNsRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsNsRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsNsRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnszone } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnszone.DnsNsRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsNsRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### DnsPtrRecord <a name="DnsPtrRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsPtrRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS PTR Record implementation.

PTR records are used for reverse DNS lookups, mapping IP addresses to hostnames.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create a PTR record:
const ptrRecord = new DnsPtrRecord(this, "ptr-record", {
  name: "50",
  dnsZoneId: reverseZone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { ptrdname: "server1.example.com" },
  ],
});
```

### DnsPtrRecord <a name="DnsPtrRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsPtrRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS PTR Record implementation.

PTR records are used for reverse DNS lookups, mapping IP addresses to hostnames.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create a PTR record:
const ptrRecord = new DnsPtrRecord(this, "ptr-record", {
  name: "50",
  dnsZoneId: reverseZone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { ptrdname: "server1.example.com" },
  ],
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsPtrRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnszone } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnszone.DnsPtrRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsPtrRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsResolver <a name="DnsResolver" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolver"></a>

Unified Azure DNS Resolver implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that replaces all
version-specific DNS Resolver classes. It automatically handles version
resolution, schema validation, and property transformation while maintaining
full backward compatibility.

Azure DNS Private Resolvers enable hybrid DNS scenarios, allowing conditional
forwarding between Azure, on-premises, and other cloud providers. They provide
DNS resolution for resources in Azure virtual networks.

Key Requirements:
- Requires a dedicated subnet with delegation to Microsoft.Network/dnsResolvers
- Subnet must be between /28 and /24 in size
- Each subscription can have up to 15 DNS resolvers
- Regional resource (unlike DNS zones which are global)

*Example*

```typescript
// DNS resolver with explicit version pinning:
const dnsResolver = new DnsResolver(this, "resolver", {
  name: "my-dns-resolver",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  virtualNetworkId: vnet.id,
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01",
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolver.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsResolver } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsResolver.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolver.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsResolver <a name="DnsResolver" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolver"></a>

Unified Azure DNS Resolver implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that replaces all
version-specific DNS Resolver classes. It automatically handles version
resolution, schema validation, and property transformation while maintaining
full backward compatibility.

Azure DNS Private Resolvers enable hybrid DNS scenarios, allowing conditional
forwarding between Azure, on-premises, and other cloud providers. They provide
DNS resolution for resources in Azure virtual networks.

Key Requirements:
- Requires a dedicated subnet with delegation to Microsoft.Network/dnsResolvers
- Subnet must be between /28 and /24 in size
- Each subscription can have up to 15 DNS resolvers
- Regional resource (unlike DNS zones which are global)

*Example*

```typescript
// DNS resolver with explicit version pinning:
const dnsResolver = new DnsResolver(this, "resolver", {
  name: "my-dns-resolver",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  virtualNetworkId: vnet.id,
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01",
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolver.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnsresolver } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolver.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolver.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### DnsResolverInboundEndpoint <a name="DnsResolverInboundEndpoint" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolverInboundEndpoint"></a>

Azure DNS Resolver Inbound Endpoint implementation.

Inbound Endpoints allow external DNS servers (such as on-premises DNS servers)
to query Azure-hosted DNS zones through the DNS Resolver. This enables hybrid
DNS scenarios where external networks need to resolve Azure private DNS zones.

Requirements:
- Dedicated subnet between /28 and /24
- Subnet must be delegated to Microsoft.Network/dnsResolvers
- Must be in the same VNet as the parent DNS Resolver
- Each DNS Resolver can have multiple inbound endpoints

*Example*

```typescript
// Inbound endpoint with tags and version pinning:
const inboundEndpoint = new DnsResolverInboundEndpoint(this, "inbound-endpoint", {
  name: "my-inbound-endpoint",
  location: "eastus",
  dnsResolverId: dnsResolver.id,
  subnetId: inboundSubnet.id,
  tags: {
    environment: "production",
    purpose: "hybrid-dns"
  },
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01"
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolverInboundEndpoint.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsResolverInboundEndpoint } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsResolverInboundEndpoint.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolverInboundEndpoint.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### DnsResolverInboundEndpoint <a name="DnsResolverInboundEndpoint" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolverInboundEndpoint"></a>

Azure DNS Resolver Inbound Endpoint implementation.

Inbound Endpoints allow external DNS servers (such as on-premises DNS servers)
to query Azure-hosted DNS zones through the DNS Resolver. This enables hybrid
DNS scenarios where external networks need to resolve Azure private DNS zones.

Requirements:
- Dedicated subnet between /28 and /24
- Subnet must be delegated to Microsoft.Network/dnsResolvers
- Must be in the same VNet as the parent DNS Resolver
- Each DNS Resolver can have multiple inbound endpoints

*Example*

```typescript
// Inbound endpoint with tags and version pinning:
const inboundEndpoint = new DnsResolverInboundEndpoint(this, "inbound-endpoint", {
  name: "my-inbound-endpoint",
  location: "eastus",
  dnsResolverId: dnsResolver.id,
  subnetId: inboundSubnet.id,
  tags: {
    environment: "production",
    purpose: "hybrid-dns"
  },
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01"
});
```

### DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint <a name="DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint"></a>

Azure DNS Resolver Outbound Endpoint implementation.

Outbound Endpoints enable Azure resources to forward DNS queries to external DNS servers
(such as on-premises DNS servers). This enables hybrid DNS scenarios where Azure resources
need to resolve names from external DNS zones.

Requirements:
- Dedicated subnet between /28 and /24
- Subnet must be delegated to Microsoft.Network/dnsResolvers
- Must be in the same VNet as the parent DNS Resolver
- Each DNS Resolver can have multiple outbound endpoints
- Outbound endpoints are used with forwarding rules to specify which queries to forward

*Example*

```typescript
// Outbound endpoint with version pinning:
const outboundEndpoint = new DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint(this, "outbound-endpoint", {
  name: "my-outbound-endpoint",
  location: "eastus",
  dnsResolverId: dnsResolver.id,
  subnetId: outboundSubnet.id,
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01"
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint <a name="DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint"></a>

Azure DNS Resolver Outbound Endpoint implementation.

Outbound Endpoints enable Azure resources to forward DNS queries to external DNS servers
(such as on-premises DNS servers). This enables hybrid DNS scenarios where Azure resources
need to resolve names from external DNS zones.

Requirements:
- Dedicated subnet between /28 and /24
- Subnet must be delegated to Microsoft.Network/dnsResolvers
- Must be in the same VNet as the parent DNS Resolver
- Each DNS Resolver can have multiple outbound endpoints
- Outbound endpoints are used with forwarding rules to specify which queries to forward

*Example*

```typescript
// Outbound endpoint with version pinning:
const outboundEndpoint = new DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint(this, "outbound-endpoint", {
  name: "my-outbound-endpoint",
  location: "eastus",
  dnsResolverId: dnsResolver.id,
  subnetId: outboundSubnet.id,
  apiVersion: "2022-07-01"
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnsresolver } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsresolver.DnsResolverOutboundEndpoint.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsSoaRecord <a name="DnsSoaRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsSoaRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS SOA Record implementation.

SOA records contain administrative information about a DNS zone.
Note: Each zone automatically has an SOA record; this is typically used to update it.

*Example*

```typescript
// Update the SOA record:
const soaRecord = new DnsSoaRecord(this, "soa-record", {
  name: "@",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  soaRecord: {
    email: "admin.example.com",
    refreshTime: 3600,
    retryTime: 300,
    expireTime: 2419200,
    minimumTTL: 300,
  },
});
```

Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsSoaRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsSoaRecord } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsSoaRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsSoaRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsSoaRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnszone } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnszone.DnsSoaRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsSoaRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### DnsSrvRecord <a name="DnsSrvRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsSrvRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS SRV Record implementation.

SRV records specify the location of services like SIP, XMPP, etc.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create an SRV record for a SIP service:
const srvRecord = new DnsSrvRecord(this, "sip-record", {
  name: "_sip._tcp",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { priority: 10, weight: 60, port: 5060, target: "sipserver1.example.com" },
    { priority: 10, weight: 40, port: 5060, target: "sipserver2.example.com" },
  ],
});
```

### DnsSrvRecord <a name="DnsSrvRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsSrvRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS SRV Record implementation.

SRV records specify the location of services like SIP, XMPP, etc.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create an SRV record for a SIP service:
const srvRecord = new DnsSrvRecord(this, "sip-record", {
  name: "_sip._tcp",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { priority: 10, weight: 60, port: 5060, target: "sipserver1.example.com" },
    { priority: 10, weight: 40, port: 5060, target: "sipserver2.example.com" },
  ],
});
```

Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsSrvRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnszone } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnszone.DnsSrvRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsSrvRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### DnsTxtRecord <a name="DnsTxtRecord" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsTxtRecord"></a>

Azure Public DNS TXT Record implementation.

TXT records store arbitrary text data, commonly used for SPF, DKIM, domain verification, etc.

*Example*

```typescript
// Create a TXT record for SPF:
const txtRecord = new DnsTxtRecord(this, "spf-record", {
  name: "@",
  dnsZoneId: zone.id,
  ttl: 3600,
  records: [
    { value: ["v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com -all"] },
  ],
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsTxtRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { DnsTxtRecord } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

DnsTxtRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsTxtRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsTxtRecord.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnszone } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnszone.DnsTxtRecord.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsTxtRecord.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### DnsZone <a name="DnsZone" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.DnsZone"></a>

Unified Azure DNS Zone implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that replaces all
version-specific DNS Zone classes. It automatically handles version
resolution, schema validation, and property transformation while maintaining
full backward compatibility.

Azure DNS Zones are global resources used to host DNS records for a domain.
They can be either Public (Internet-accessible) or Private (accessible only
from specified virtual networks).

*Example*

```typescript
// DNS zone with explicit version pinning:
const dnsZone = new DnsZone(this, "dns", {
  name: "contoso.com",
  location: "global",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  apiVersion: "2018-05-01",
});
```

### DnsZone <a name="DnsZone" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsZone"></a>

Unified Azure DNS Zone implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that replaces all
version-specific DNS Zone classes. It automatically handles version
resolution, schema validation, and property transformation while maintaining
full backward compatibility.

Azure DNS Zones are global resources used to host DNS records for a domain.
They can be either Public (Internet-accessible) or Private (accessible only
from specified virtual networks).

*Example*

```typescript
// DNS zone with explicit version pinning:
const dnsZone = new DnsZone(this, "dns", {
  name: "contoso.com",
  location: "global",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  apiVersion: "2018-05-01",
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsZone.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnszone } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnszone.DnsZone.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnszone.DnsZone.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.EventGridEventSubscription.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { EventGridEventSubscription } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

EventGridEventSubscription.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.EventGridEventSubscription.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_eventgrideventsubscription.EventGridEventSubscription.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.


Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_eventgridsystemtopic.EventGridSystemTopic.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_eventgridsystemtopic } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_eventgridsystemtopic.EventGridSystemTopic.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_eventgridsystemtopic.EventGridSystemTopic.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### Eventhub <a name="Eventhub" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.Eventhub"></a>

Azure Event Hub (entity) implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that automatically
handles version resolution, schema validation, and property transformation
while maintaining full JSII compliance.

**Child Resource Pattern**: Event Hubs are child resources of Event Hubs
Namespaces. This implementation overrides the `resolveParentId()` method to
properly construct the namespace ID as the parent.

*Example*

```typescript
// Event Hub with an explicit namespace reference (creates a dependency):
const hub = new Eventhub(this, "my-hub", {
  name: "my-event-hub",
  namespaceName: namespace.props.name!,
  namespaceId: namespace.id,
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.Eventhub.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { Eventhub } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

Eventhub.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.Eventhub.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### Eventhub <a name="Eventhub" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_eventhub.Eventhub"></a>

Azure Event Hub (entity) implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that automatically
handles version resolution, schema validation, and property transformation
while maintaining full JSII compliance.

**Child Resource Pattern**: Event Hubs are child resources of Event Hubs
Namespaces. This implementation overrides the `resolveParentId()` method to
properly construct the namespace ID as the parent.

*Example*

```typescript
// Event Hub with an explicit namespace reference (creates a dependency):
const hub = new Eventhub(this, "my-hub", {
  name: "my-event-hub",
  namespaceName: namespace.props.name!,
  namespaceId: namespace.id,
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
});
```

##### `addTag` <a name="addTag" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_eventhub.Eventhub.addTag"></a>

```typescript
public addTag(key: string, value: string): void
```

Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

### EventhubNamespace <a name="EventhubNamespace" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.EventhubNamespace"></a>

Azure Event Hubs Namespace implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that automatically
handles version resolution, schema validation, and property transformation
while maintaining full JSII compliance.

An Event Hubs Namespace is a management container for Event Hubs. It provides
DNS-integrated network endpoints and a range of access control and network
integration management features.

*Example*

```typescript
// Standard namespace with auto-inflate:
const namespace = new EventhubNamespace(this, "production-namespace", {
  name: "prod-eventhub-ns",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  sku: { name: "Standard", capacity: 2 },
  isAutoInflateEnabled: true,
  maximumThroughputUnits: 10,
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.EventhubNamespace.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { EventhubNamespace } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

EventhubNamespace.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.EventhubNamespace.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_eventhub.EventhubNamespace.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_eventhub } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_eventhub.EventhubNamespace.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_eventhub.EventhubNamespace.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### ForwardingRule <a name="ForwardingRule" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.ForwardingRule"></a>

Azure DNS Forwarding Rule implementation.

Forwarding rules define conditional DNS forwarding behavior. When a DNS query
matches the domain name pattern, it's forwarded to the specified target DNS servers.
Up to 1000 rules can be configured per ruleset, with up to 6 target servers per rule.

*Example*

```typescript
// Disabled forwarding rule:
const rule = new ForwardingRule(this, "rule", {
  name: "temp-rule",
  dnsForwardingRulesetId: ruleset.id,
  domainName: "temp.local.",
  targetDnsServers: [{ ipAddress: "10.0.0.4" }],
  forwardingRuleState: "Disabled"
});
```


Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

### ForwardingRule <a name="ForwardingRule" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsforwardingruleset.ForwardingRule"></a>

Azure DNS Forwarding Rule implementation.

Forwarding rules define conditional DNS forwarding behavior. When a DNS query
matches the domain name pattern, it's forwarded to the specified target DNS servers.
Up to 1000 rules can be configured per ruleset, with up to 6 target servers per rule.

*Example*

```typescript
// Disabled forwarding rule:
const rule = new ForwardingRule(this, "rule", {
  name: "temp-rule",
  dnsForwardingRulesetId: ruleset.id,
  domainName: "temp.local.",
  targetDnsServers: [{ ipAddress: "10.0.0.4" }],
  forwardingRuleState: "Disabled"
});
```


Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsforwardingruleset.ForwardingRule.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_dnsforwardingruleset } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_dnsforwardingruleset.ForwardingRule.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_dnsforwardingruleset.ForwardingRule.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### FunctionApp <a name="FunctionApp" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.FunctionApp"></a>

Unified Azure Function App implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that replaces all
version-specific Function App classes. It automatically handles version
resolution, schema validation, and property transformation while maintaining
full backward compatibility.

*Example*

```typescript
// Function App with managed identity:
const functionApp = new FunctionApp(this, "func", {
  name: "my-function-app",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  serverFarmId: appServicePlan.id,
  kind: "functionapp,linux",
  identity: {
    type: "SystemAssigned",
  },
  httpsOnly: true,
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.FunctionApp.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { FunctionApp } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

FunctionApp.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.FunctionApp.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### FunctionApp <a name="FunctionApp" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_functionapp.FunctionApp"></a>

Unified Azure Function App implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that replaces all
version-specific Function App classes. It automatically handles version
resolution, schema validation, and property transformation while maintaining
full backward compatibility.

*Example*

```typescript
// Function App with managed identity:
const functionApp = new FunctionApp(this, "func", {
  name: "my-function-app",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  serverFarmId: appServicePlan.id,
  kind: "functionapp,linux",
  identity: {
    type: "SystemAssigned",
  },
  httpsOnly: true,
});
```

### IpamPool <a name="IpamPool" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.IpamPool"></a>

Azure Virtual Network Manager IPAM Pool implementation.

IPAM Pools provide centralized IP address management for virtual networks,
enabling automatic CIDR allocation, overlap prevention, and hierarchical
address space organization. They are essential for managing IP addresses
at scale across multiple virtual networks and subscriptions.

*Example*

```typescript
// Hierarchical pool with parent reference:
const childPool = new IpamPool(this, "eastus-pool", {
  name: "eastus-pool",
  location: "eastus",
  networkManagerId: networkManager.id,
  addressPrefixes: ["10.1.0.0/16"],
  parentPoolName: "production-pool",
  description: "East US regional pool"
});
```

```typescript

```

Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.IpamPool.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { IpamPool } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

IpamPool.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.IpamPool.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### IpamPool <a name="IpamPool" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_virtualnetworkmanager.IpamPool"></a>

Azure Virtual Network Manager IPAM Pool implementation.

IPAM Pools provide centralized IP address management for virtual networks,
enabling automatic CIDR allocation, overlap prevention, and hierarchical
address space organization. They are essential for managing IP addresses
at scale across multiple virtual networks and subscriptions.

*Example*

```typescript
// Hierarchical pool with parent reference:
const childPool = new IpamPool(this, "eastus-pool", {
  name: "eastus-pool",
  location: "eastus",
  networkManagerId: networkManager.id,
  addressPrefixes: ["10.1.0.0/16"],
  parentPoolName: "production-pool",
  description: "East US regional pool"
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_virtualnetworkmanager.IpamPool.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_virtualnetworkmanager } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_virtualnetworkmanager.IpamPool.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_virtualnetworkmanager.IpamPool.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### IpamPoolStaticCidr <a name="IpamPoolStaticCidr" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.IpamPoolStaticCidr"></a>

Azure Virtual Network Manager IPAM Pool Static CIDR implementation.

Static CIDRs explicitly allocate IP address blocks within an IPAM pool,
providing precise control over address space reservations. This is useful
for manual IP address management or reserving specific ranges for particular
purposes within the larger pool.

*Example*

```typescript
// Allocate with explicit IP count:
const staticCidr = new IpamPoolStaticCidr(this, "database-servers", {
  name: "db-servers-cidr",
  ipamPoolId: ipamPool.id,
  addressPrefixes: ["10.0.2.0/24"],
  description: "Reserved for database servers",
  apiVersion: "2024-05-01"
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.IpamPoolStaticCidr.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { IpamPoolStaticCidr } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

IpamPoolStaticCidr.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.IpamPoolStaticCidr.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### IpamPoolStaticCidr <a name="IpamPoolStaticCidr" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_virtualnetworkmanager.IpamPoolStaticCidr"></a>

Azure Virtual Network Manager IPAM Pool Static CIDR implementation.

Static CIDRs explicitly allocate IP address blocks within an IPAM pool,
providing precise control over address space reservations. This is useful
for manual IP address management or reserving specific ranges for particular
purposes within the larger pool.

*Example*

```typescript
// Allocate with explicit IP count:
const staticCidr = new IpamPoolStaticCidr(this, "database-servers", {
  name: "db-servers-cidr",
  ipamPoolId: ipamPool.id,
  addressPrefixes: ["10.0.2.0/24"],
  description: "Reserved for database servers",
  apiVersion: "2024-05-01"
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_virtualnetworkmanager.IpamPoolStaticCidr.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_virtualnetworkmanager } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_virtualnetworkmanager.IpamPoolStaticCidr.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_virtualnetworkmanager.IpamPoolStaticCidr.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

---

### KeyVault <a name="KeyVault" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.KeyVault"></a>

Unified Azure Key Vault implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that automatically
handles version resolution, schema validation, and property transformation
while maintaining full JSII compliance.

Azure Key Vault is a cloud service for securely storing and accessing secrets,
keys, and certificates with centralized management and access control.

*Example*

```typescript
// Usage with explicit version pinning and configuration:
const keyVault = new KeyVault(this, "kv", {
  name: "my-keyvault-1234",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  sku: { name: "premium" },
  apiVersion: "2023-07-01",
  enablePurgeProtection: true,
  publicNetworkAccess: "Disabled",
  networkAcls: {
    defaultAction: "Deny",
    bypass: "AzureServices",
  },
});
```

### KeyVault <a name="KeyVault" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_keyvault.KeyVault"></a>

Unified Azure Key Vault implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that automatically
handles version resolution, schema validation, and property transformation
while maintaining full JSII compliance.

Azure Key Vault is a cloud service for securely storing and accessing secrets,
keys, and certificates with centralized management and access control.

*Example*

```typescript
// Usage with explicit version pinning and configuration:
const keyVault = new KeyVault(this, "kv", {
  name: "my-keyvault-1234",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  sku: { name: "premium" },
  apiVersion: "2023-07-01",
  enablePurgeProtection: true,
  publicNetworkAccess: "Disabled",
  networkAcls: {
    defaultAction: "Deny",
    bypass: "AzureServices",
  },
});
```

##### `isConstruct` <a name="isConstruct" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_keyvault.KeyVault.isConstruct"></a>

```typescript
import { azure_keyvault } from '@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs'

azure_keyvault.KeyVault.isConstruct(x: any)
```

Checks if `x` is a construct.

Use this method instead of `instanceof` to properly detect `Construct`
instances, even when the construct library is symlinked.

Explanation: in JavaScript, multiple copies of the `constructs` library on
disk are seen as independent, completely different libraries. As a
consequence, the class `Construct` in each copy of the `constructs` library
is seen as a different class, and an instance of one class will not test as
`instanceof` the other class. `npm install` will not create installations
like this, but users may manually symlink construct libraries together or
use a monorepo tool: in those cases, multiple copies of the `constructs`
library can be accidentally installed, and `instanceof` will behave
unpredictably. It is safest to avoid using `instanceof`, and using
this type-testing method instead.

###### `x`<sup>Required</sup> <a name="x" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.azure_keyvault.KeyVault.isConstruct.parameter.x"></a>

- *Type:* any

Any object.

### LogAnalyticsWorkspace <a name="LogAnalyticsWorkspace" id="@microsoft/terraform-cdk-constructs.LogAnalyticsWorkspace"></a>

Unified Azure Log Analytics Workspace implementation.

This class provides a single, version-aware implementation that automatically handles version
resolution, schema validation, and property transformation while maintaining full JSII compliance.

Log Analytics Workspace is the central destination for log data from Azure resources,
applications, and on-premises infrastructure. It enables querying, analysis, and
visualization of log data using Kusto Query Language (KQL).

*Example*

```typescript
// Log Analytics Workspace with capacity reservation:
const workspace = new LogAnalyticsWorkspace(this, "high-volume-workspace", {
  name: "high-volume-logs",
  location: "eastus",
  resourceGroupId: resourceGroup.id,
  retentionInDays: 365,
  sku: {
    name: "CapacityReservation",
    capacityReservationLevel: 500
  },
  workspaceCapping: {
    dailyQuotaGb: 100
  }
});
```

Adds a tag to this resource. The tag will be included in the Azure resource.

This method provides proper immutability by storing tags separately from props.
Tags added via this method are combined with tags from props and included in
the deployed Azure resource.

**Important:** In CDK for Terraform, tags should ideally be set during resource
construction via props. While this method allows adding tags after construction,
those tags are only included if added before the Terraform configuration is
synthesized. For best results, add all tags via props or call addTag() in the
same scope where the resource is created.
